title: David Robinson says a sense of 'cognitive dissonance' led him to leave OpenAI
key_facts: David Robinson, formerly a leader on OpenAI's Safety Systems team, gave his first interview since quitting 'last week' to Ezra Klein for The New York Times' 'The Ezra Klein Show'.
He said OpenAI kept publishing warnings about dangerous models while still training and deploying them.
He described 'frenetic' activity inside OpenAI, with people 'running on fumes'.
In July hundreds of OpenAI employees signed an open letter, 'Pacing the Frontier', urging regulation to slow AI development.
In September Sam Altman said he agreed with Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei that AI development should be paced, saying 'We need to pace the frontier.'
An OpenAI spokesperson said the company pauses training or holds back models when it needs to slow down.
quote_evidence: "Part of what was the fundamental cognitive dissonance for me was we keep publishing these warnings, but ultimately, we're still training and deploying these dangerous models that we're warning about," Robinson said.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this article.
why_it_matters_hint: A former safety-team leader says OpenAI's public warnings did not match its training and deployment pace.
event_date: Interview date not stated (Business Insider dated 7 Oct 2026); quit 'last week'
notes: Source chain: Business Insider reports on the Ezra Klein interview (The New York Times podcast); the interview itself is the first report. OpenAI's comment came from an earlier spokesperson statement quoted in the article.
